## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes the calibration, field operation, and maintenance
of standalone handheld dissolved oxygen (DO) meters for in situ
measurement of dissolved oxygen concentration and percent saturation
in surface waters. Dissolved oxygen is a fundamental indicator of
water quality and aquatic habitat condition. This SOP covers optical
(luminescent) and electrochemical (polarographic and galvanic) DO
probes operated as standalone instruments, separate from multiparameter
sondes.


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Handheld DO meters (e.g., YSI Pro20i, YSI ProSolo,
  Hach HQ40d with LDO probe, Extech DO600) used for in situ DO
  measurements at EA Program surface water field sites
- **Does not apply to:** DO measured by the Eureka Manta2 multiprobe
  (see [SOP-F200](SOP-F200-eureka-manta2.qmd)); Winkler titration
  (laboratory method); BOD analysis (see future SOP-L306); continuous
  DO monitoring with deployed sondes
- **Location:** All EA Program surface water field sites


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve instrument selection; review QC data            |
| Trained Personnel | Calibrate and operate the meter per this SOP            |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use                |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Measuring DO requires placing the probe in or near
  water. Slip, fall, and drowning hazards apply. Work in pairs at
  stream sites.
- **Chemical:** Some polarographic DO probes use KCl electrolyte
  solution, which is a mild irritant.
- **Biological:** Water may contain pathogens. Avoid ingestion;
  wash hands after field work.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or wading boots
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (especially for impaired waters)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd).


## 5. Instrument Types

### 5.1 Optical (Luminescent) DO Probes

Optical probes (e.g., Hach LDO, YSI ProSolo ODO) measure DO by
detecting the quenching of luminescence from a sensing element by
oxygen molecules. They require no electrolyte, no warm-up time, no
stirring, and no membrane replacement.

| Advantage                         | Limitation                           |
|:----------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|
| No membrane to replace            | Higher initial cost                  |
| No electrolyte                    | Sensing cap has a finite lifespan (typically 1--2 years) |
| No stirring required              |                                      |
| Faster stabilization              |                                      |
| Lower maintenance                 |                                      |

### 5.2 Electrochemical (Polarographic / Galvanic) DO Probes

Electrochemical probes (e.g., YSI Pro20i) measure DO through an
oxygen-permeable membrane covering an electrode that produces a
current proportional to DO concentration. They require periodic
membrane and electrolyte replacement and a brief warm-up period.

| Advantage                         | Limitation                           |
|:----------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|
| Lower cost                        | Requires membrane replacement        |
| Well-established method           | Requires electrolyte refill          |
| Widely available                  | Needs 5--15 min warm-up              |
|                                   | Flow-dependent (stirring or moving water needed) |

## 6. Equipment and Materials

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Handheld DO meter with probe          | Fully charged; confirm calibration supplies |
| Water-saturated air calibration chamber | Typically a wet sponge in the probe storage cap |
| Barometric pressure reference         | Built into some meters; otherwise use a Kestrel or phone app |
| Spare membranes and electrolyte (electrochemical probes) | Keep in the field kit |
| Spare sensing cap (optical probes)    | Replace when expired or readings become erratic |
| Thermometer (for verification)        | Most DO probes include temperature; useful for cross-check |
| DI water (squeeze bottle)             | For rinsing the probe                    |
| Lint-free wipes                       | For drying the probe before calibration  |
| Field notebook                        | For recording calibration and measurements |
| Spare batteries                       | Matched to meter model                   |


## 7. Procedure

### 7.1 Calibration

Calibrate the DO meter before each field day. The most common
calibration method is the **water-saturated air** method, which is
simple, reliable, and does not require chemical reagents.

**Water-saturated air calibration:**

1. Ensure the calibration chamber (probe storage cap with a damp
   sponge) contains a moist sponge. The sponge should be damp but not
   dripping; the probe tip should not touch the sponge or water.
2. Turn on the meter. For electrochemical probes, allow a warm-up
   period of 5--15 minutes (consult the manual for your model).
3. Enter the current barometric pressure (in mmHg or hPa). Some
   meters auto-sense pressure; verify the displayed value against a
   Kestrel or weather station.
4. Place the probe in the calibration chamber and wait for the reading
   to stabilize (1--3 minutes for optical probes; 5--10 minutes for
   electrochemical probes).
5. Press **Cal** (or follow the on-screen calibration prompts). The
   meter adjusts to 100% saturation at the current temperature and
   pressure.
6. Record in the field notebook: calibration date, time, barometric
   pressure, temperature, and whether the calibration was accepted.

**Zero-oxygen calibration (optional, for low-DO environments):**

1. Prepare a zero-oxygen solution by dissolving excess sodium sulfite
   (Na~2~SO~3~) in DI water with a pinch of cobalt chloride catalyst.
2. Immerse the probe and wait for the reading to stabilize.
3. Calibrate the zero point per the meter instructions.
4. This step is recommended when expected DO values are below 2 mg/L.

### 7.2 Field Measurement

1. At the sampling location, immerse the probe to mid-depth in the
   water column. For electrochemical probes, maintain a minimum flow
   of 0.3 m/s past the membrane (gently move the probe back and forth
   in still water). Optical probes do not require flow.
2. Wait for the reading to stabilize (the display will indicate
   "stable" or the reading will stop fluctuating).
3. Record in the field notebook:
   - DO concentration (mg/L)
   - DO percent saturation (%)
   - Water temperature (C), as reported by the probe
   - Date, time, and sample ID
   - Measurement depth
   - Flow conditions (e.g., "riffle," "pool," "still water with
     manual stirring")
4. If measuring at multiple depths (e.g., lake profiling), lower the
   probe in 0.5 or 1.0 m increments and allow the reading to
   stabilize at each depth. Record depth, DO, and temperature for
   each measurement.

### 7.3 Post-Field Care

1. Rinse the probe with DI water after each use.
2. For electrochemical probes, check the membrane for tears, bubbles,
   or deposits. Replace the membrane and electrolyte if damaged.
3. For optical probes, gently wipe the sensing cap with a soft, damp
   cloth if biofouling is visible. Do not use solvents.
4. Store the probe in the calibration chamber with a moist sponge (not
   submerged in water).
5. Turn off the meter to conserve battery. Remove batteries if storing
   for more than one month.


## 8. Data Interpretation

DO concentrations in surface waters are influenced by temperature,
atmospheric pressure, salinity, photosynthesis, respiration, and
reaeration. General reference values for freshwater:

| DO (mg/L) | Condition                              |
|:----------|:---------------------------------------|
| > 8       | Well-oxygenated; suitable for most aquatic life |
| 5--8      | Adequate for many species; marginal for cold-water fish |
| 2--5      | Stressful for most fish; hypoxic conditions |
| < 2       | Severe hypoxia; lethal to most aquatic organisms |

DO saturation near 100% indicates equilibrium with the atmosphere.
Supersaturation (> 100%) often indicates active photosynthesis; values
well below 100% suggest high biological oxygen demand or poor
reaeration.


## 9. Quality Control

- Calibrate at the start of each field day (Section 7.1).
- At the end of the field day, check the calibration by placing the
  probe in the water-saturated air chamber. The reading should be
  within +/- 2% of 100% saturation. If it has drifted more than 5%,
  note the drift and recalibrate; consider re-measuring recent
  samples.
- When possible, verify the probe against a second DO meter or the
  Eureka Manta2 by measuring the same water body. Readings should
  agree within +/- 0.5 mg/L.
- For long field days (> 6 hours), perform a mid-day calibration check.
- Record all QC results in the field notebook.

## 12. Training Record

Before using DO meters independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Demonstrate a complete water-saturated air calibration
3. Perform supervised DO measurements at one field site
4. Demonstrate proper membrane inspection and replacement (for
   electrochemical probes) or sensing cap inspection (for optical
   probes)
5. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
